Closing Thought

Not every CU behaves the same way, and not all consumption is immediately obvious. But most of what you see on your Capacity Dashboard can be linked to a provisioning decision, a flow design choice, or an optional service that was enabled. The more intentional those decisions are, the fewer surprises you will find.

You now have the map. Use the Estimator to plan, the Capacity Dashboard to monitor, and the decision table in Section 8 as your checklist every time a new service is proposed.

entry.title: Data Access Control (DAC) Scenarios in SAP Datasphere
entry.content:
This document demonstrates multiple Data Access Control (DAC) scenarios using different combinations of State and Category filters. Its purpose is to explain how DAC works across multiple scenarios and how access rules can be designed according to specific business requirements. Based on the requirement, permission tables can be created and DACs can then be defined using those permission tables. The cases show how single and multiple DACs behave, including OR and AND logic, unrestricted values, exclusions, overlapping access groups, and conflicting rules that return no data. Screenshots are included to illustrate each configuration and its result.

Implementation steps:

Step 1: Create the permission table.

Step 2: Create the DAC based on the permission table.

Step 3: Assign the DAC to the relevant views or analytical models.

I have not included detailed instructions for Steps 1 to 3 because they are already covered in many blogs on the SAP Community. This document assumes that readers working with SAP Datasphere are familiar with creating permission tables and DACs and assigning DACs to views or analytical models.

Refer this link for best practices : https://help.sap.com/docs/SAP_DATASPHERE/be5967d099974c69b77f4549425ca4c0/a032e51c730147c7a1fcac125b4cfe14.html?locale=en-US#loioa032e51c730147c7a1fcac125b4cfe14__section_best_practices

Note: As a best practice, create a dedicated permission space to store permission tables. Govern access by sharing the space only with the appropriate developers who are responsible for maintaining row-level security.

Dataset: The examples use the open Sales Data Set available on Kaggle.

Testing and privacy note: Each case was tested using a single User ID. User ID is hidden in the screenshots because they are personal information.

In Sales Dataset , we have state and Category dimensions holding data for multiple US states and multiple Categories.

 

Case 1: State = California or Alabama and Category = Furniture

 

To show data where State = California and Category = Furniture OR State = Alabama and Category = Furniture

Condition

(State = California AND Category = Furniture)

OR

(State = Alabama AND Category = Furniture)

SAC output 

 

Case 2: All California Categories or Alabama Furniture

Condition

(State = California AND Category = *)

OR

(State = Alabama AND Category = Furniture)

 

SAC

 

Case 3: All Categories for California or Alabama

Condition

(State = California AND Category = *)

OR

(State = Alabama AND Category = *)

 

Case 4: Combining Two DACs on the Same View

DAC 1 ( Type Operator and Values )

Condition :

(State EQ Alabama AND Category = *)

 OR (State EQ California AND Category = *)

DAC 2 (Type Single Only)

Condition:

(State EQ Alabama AND Category = Furniture)

 OR (State EQ California AND Category = Furniture)

Explanation: When two DACs are assigned to the same view, they are combined using AND logic. A row is shown only if both DACs allow it; therefore, the more restrictive DAC takes precedence.

Result: SAC will show California Furniture or Alabama Furniture.

 

Case 5: States from Alabama to California, Excluding Arizona

 

Requirement: User A should see states from Alabama to California, excluding Arizona

Explanation: The configuration below excludes Arizona and all categories associated with it.

 

Case 6: All States and Categories Except California Furniture

 

Requirement: Show all states and categories except the Furniture category for California.

 

 

Case 7: California with All Categories

 

Explanation: This is an alternative configuration in which the Category does not need to be specified explicitly.

SAC

 

Case 8: Overlapping Groups Without Duplicate Rows

 

Requirement: Show California with all categories, together with all states that have the Furniture category.

Explanation: Group 1 and Group 2 overlap, but the overlap does not create duplicate rows.

 

 

Case 9: Conflicting DACs Assigned to One View

DAC 1 ( Type  : Single value ) : Show State = Alabama and Category = Furniture.

DAC 2 Type ( Operator and values ) : Show State = California and Category = All.

Result: If DAC 1 and DAC 2 are both assigned to a single view, no data will be shown.

Explanation: Each row must satisfy both DACs. DAC 1 allows only Alabama, while DAC 2 allows only California. Because a row cannot belong to both states at the same time, no rows pass the combined filter.

 

Comparison with SAP BW Analysis Authorizations

 

>Aggregation Authorisation in SAP BW

In SAP BW, aggregation authorisation using the colon (:) can allow a user to view an aggregated result for a characteristic without granting access to its individual values. SAP Datasphere DACs work differently: they apply row-level filters, removing unauthorised records before the result is aggregated.

Example

 

Cost Center

Employee

Salary

CC100

Mark

100

CC100

Bob

100

CC100

John

100

SAP BW result: With “:” authorisation for Employee, the user can run a query by Cost Center and view the complete aggregated value for CC100: 300.

If the user drills down by Employee, SAP BW blocks access to the individual employee values. The user can therefore see the full total without viewing the underlying salary details.

SAP Datasphere DAC result: A DAC filters out rows that the user is not authorised to access. If the user is authorised to view only Mark’s record, the rows for Bob and John are excluded before aggregation. The value shown for CC100 is therefore 100.

Key takeaway: SAP BW Analysis Authorizations can support aggregated reporting while restricting access to lower-level characteristic values. A SAP Datasphere DAC controls which rows are available to the user, so excluded rows do not contribute to the aggregate. A standard DAC therefore does not provide the same behaviour as BW aggregation authorisation.

>Key-figure (column-level) security:

 SAP BW can restrict key figures through 1KYFNM, allowing sensitive measures to be hidden from selected users. SAP Datasphere DACs provide row-level security only. To achieve a similar separation in SAP Datasphere, separate analytical models may be required for different user groups.

>Hierarchy authorisations:

SAP BW supports authorisation at hierarchy-node level, including level restrictions, aggregated-only display, and hierarchy versions and validity dates. SAP Datasphere offers more limited hierarchy-based access control through DACs.

>Define once and enforce broadly:

In SAP BW, an authorisation-relevant characteristic is checked across the InfoProviders and queries that use it. In SAP Datasphere, a DAC must be assigned to each relevant view or analytical model. If a required assignment is missed, the data may remain unprotected.

Summary 

SAP Datasphere DACs are well suited to straightforward row-level filtering at scale. SAP BW Analysis Authorizations are stronger where the requirement includes partial visibility, such as totals without underlying details, hidden key figures, or more advanced hierarchy authorisations, as well as strict audit and compliance controls. In a migration from SAP BW to SAP Datasphere, aggregation authorisations and key-figure authorisations require deliberate redesign rather than a one-to-one mapping.

entry.title: SAP TechEd 2026: Must-Attend Sessions for Data Professionals
entry.content:
SAP TechEd 2026 (October 27–29) offers no shortage of sessions on data, AI, architecture, and analytics. The harder question is which ones deserve a place on your agenda. With SAP Business Data Cloud now in production and AI capabilities expanding across the SAP portfolio, this year’s most valuable sessions should help you, the practitioner, move beyond product updates to make better decisions about what to build, govern, modernize, and scale.

This blog narrows the field to the sessions I believe are most relevant for five data and AI practitioner personas: Enterprise Architects, Data Stewards, Data Engineers, Data Analysts, and Data Scientists. The selections emphasize practical takeaways, from designing governed data foundations and modernizing pipelines to enabling trusted, context-rich AI, so you can focus on the sessions most likely to inform your next project.

Whether attending in-person or virtual start building your agenda now — choose the sessions that match your role and share your must-attend picks with peers in the Data and AI Professionals community to keep the conversation and practical learning going well beyond the event.

This list reflects my own picks, so I've likely missed a few gems. If there's a session you're planning to attend that didn't make the cut, drop it in the comments — I'd love to know what's on your radar.

 

Keynotes

KEY100 | Built for the ones who build

KEY100V | Built for the ones who build (virtual)

Why Attend

SAP TechEd's opening keynote answers the question every architect and practitioner is asking: what can I actually build on SAP's AI platform today? SAP unifies AI, business data, governance, agents, and a new UX layer into one integrated platform — eliminating manual data pipelines, model training overhead, and unpredictable AI costs. Hear directly from SAP leadership what is production-ready now and leave with a clear picture of the business outcomes you can start delivering immediately.

Key Takeaways

  • SAP Business AI Platform unifies AI, data, governance, agents, and UX into one platform — eliminating manual pipeline setup, training overhead, and unpredictable infrastructure costs.
  • Designed so developers, architects, and practitioners focus on building outcomes, not managing underlying complexity.
  • For IT leaders evaluating adoption timelines, this session defines what is production-ready now versus what is on the horizon.

 

KEY101 | Agent v0.0.7 - A license to skill

KEY101V | Agent v0.0.7 - A license to skill (virtual)

Why Attend

Master the AI-driven development revolution. Join Agent Kasimir to see how SAP Business AI Platform, Joule Studio, and open ecosystem tools empower practitioners in AI-driven development. The session shows data professionals how agentic orchestration and context-aware AI work together — redefining how enterprise solutions are built across SAP and non-SAP environments. Evaluating how AI agents fit your analytics workflows? This session moves you from concept to action.

Key Takeaways

  • Joule Studio gives practitioners a supported entry point to build and orchestrate enterprise-grounded AI agents — without starting from scratch.
  • Data professionals get a path to AI workflows where agents reason over business data, coordinate, and integrate across SAP and non-SAP tools.
  • SAP's agentic AI is built on openness — ecosystem tools sit first-class alongside SAP-native capabilities, amplifying existing investments, not displacing them.

 

Enterprise Architects

ST135 | Agent interoperability: Protocols, patterns, and enterprise strategy

Why Attend

As multi-agent AI reaches enterprise scale, interoperability becomes an architectural imperative — this strategy session delivers the protocol-level knowledge architects and developers need. It covers open standards and integration patterns, including A2A and MCP, enabling secure, composable agent networks across SAP and third-party platforms. Leave with the foundation for enterprise-scale AI architectures designed to interoperate — not just orchestrate.

Key Takeaways

  • Agent2Agent (A2A) defines how AI agents from different vendors communicate — the foundational protocol for multi-agent networks spanning SAP and third-party systems.
  • MCP governs agent access to enterprise tools and APIs — mastering A2A and MCP together is essential for reliable cross-platform architectures at enterprise scale.
  • The session delivers practical patterns for building secure, composable agent networks across SAP and non-SAP — a blueprint for expanding agent ecosystems confidently.

 

XP113 | Build AI agents on SAP and non-SAP data and context in an open lakehouse

Why Attend

If your organization is evaluating SAP Business Data Cloud with Dremio, this is the technical blueprint for building AI agents that reason across your full data estate without siloed or ungoverned copies. The session shows how architects and developers use Apache Iceberg and Apache Polaris to integrate SAP and third-party data in an open lakehouse — creating governed data products and ontologies that power Joule agents and enable external consumption through A2A. You'll leave with a clear, end-to-end path from unified data to production-ready agentic AI.

Key Takeaways

  • An open lakehouse on Apache Iceberg and Apache Polaris unifies SAP and third-party data into a single governed layer — giving AI agents real-time access to the full data estate without movement, duplication, or governance compromise.
  • Zero-copy access ensures AI agents always reason over current, authoritative data — reducing management overhead while keeping security and compliance controls intact.
  • A2A protocols extend governed data products beyond SAP boundaries — giving architects a composable foundation where Joule and third-party agents access business context through standardized, controlled interfaces.

 

RA110 | Joule and SAP Knowledge Graph: Context-aware AI across SAP solutions

RA110V | Joule and SAP Knowledge Graph: Context-aware AI across SAP solutions (virtual)

Why Attend

Context separates a generically intelligent AI from one that truly understands your business — this session reveals how SAP AI Core, the orchestration layer behind Joule, delivers that context at scale. You’ll learn how to extend Joule Agents, leverage the Joule Studio model library, connect SAP Business Data Cloud data products, and embed AI directly in SAP S/4HANA. For professionals designing AI agent architectures or SAP analytics integrations, this is where governance, context, and intelligence converge in a production-ready architecture.

Key Takeaways

  • SAP AI Core is the orchestration layer that governs how Joule agents access models, coordinate reasoning, and embed AI directly into SAP S/4HANA within a fully auditable architecture.
  • Joule agents ground every action in trusted data via SAP Business Data Cloud and AI Core, while SAP Knowledge Graph anchors reasoning in real business relationships — delivering business-aware decisions, not generic predictions.
  • The result is an AI architecture where context, governance, and intelligence are built in by design — giving architects a production-ready foundation for extending Joule across analytics, planning, and S/4HANA use cases.

 

Data Stewards

ST200 | The next evolution of SAP Business Data Cloud with Dremio and SAP Reltio

Why Attend

SAP’s 2026 acquisitions of Dremio and Reltio are reshaping Business Data Cloud’s data fabric — this session gives architects and stewards the full picture on governance, master data quality, and the trusted foundation agentic AI requires — and what your organization needs to act on now.

Key Takeaways

  • Dremio’s Iceberg-native integration extends Business Data Cloud into an enterprise lakehouse — giving AI agents zero-copy access to current, authoritative SAP and non-SAP data while preserving governance.
  • SAP Reltio delivers AI-native MDM to Business Data Cloud — harmonizing trusted golden records across data domains so agents have the consistent reference layer they need to reason reliably in production.
  • Together, Dremio and Reltio close enterprise AI’s two critical gaps — unified data access without duplication, and trusted master data quality — delivering the governed foundation agentic AI demands at scale.

 

XP826 | Get a road map to your data products foundation: Powering AI outcomes

Why Attend

AI agents deliver value only when they know what data exists, where it lives, and whether it can be trusted. This session gives architects and stewards a practical road map for integrating governance, quality, and context to make enterprise data AI-ready — so agents can query the right information at scale to drive measurable outcomes.

Key Takeaways

  • Trusted data foundations require ongoing discipline — governance, quality, and semantic context at every layer so agents can discover, assess, and act with confidence.
  • Governance, quality, and context must travel with the data — keeping agents within defined trust boundaries wherever data resides.
  • Data products — governed, reusable, context-enriched units — are the building block for scaling AI outcomes, letting multiple agents consume trusted data without duplicating governance effort.

 

DA104 | Reimagining master data as the foundation for enterprise AI

Why Attend

AI agents grounded in inconsistent or ungoverned master data produce unreliable outcomes — this session reframes MDM as the strategic prerequisite for trusted AI at scale. See how SAP Business Data Cloud unifies, governs, and delivers master data as reusable products that ground analytics, autonomous applications, and AI agents in consistent, trustworthy business context.

Key Takeaways

  • Structured master data products keep agents grounded in consistent, authoritative context — eliminating the inconsistency that causes unreliable or contradictory outputs in production.
  • Data stewards now hold a critical AI risk role — the governance rules, quality thresholds, and semantic metadata they define directly determine agent accuracy and auditability.
  • Master data quality is a strategic AI enabler, not just an operational concern — organizations investing in governed master data through SAP Business Data Cloud will deploy reliable, scalable agentic AI ahead of those that do not.

 

Data Engineers

DA100 | Enhancing agentic AI with trusted business data 

DA100V | Enhancing agentic AI with trusted business data (virtual)

Why Attend

This session answers a critical enterprise AI question: how do you ensure agents access accurate, governed, and contextually rich business data? Learn how SAP Business Data Cloud’s zero-copy architecture enables AI agents to consume trusted enterprise data in place — reducing data movement while maintaining the security, compliance, and control production AI demands.

Key Takeaways

  • Zero-copy architecture gives AI agents in-place access to enterprise data — eliminating movement and duplication while keeping governance controls fully intact.
  • Data product-level governance ensures context, permissions, and semantic meaning travel with the data — making agent outputs trustworthy and auditable by design, not retrospective monitoring.
  • Together, zero-copy access and data product-level governance shift AI quality assurance from reactive to proactive — giving architects a scalable, compliance-ready foundation for deploying agents with confidence.

 

DA200 | Agentic SAP BW modernization: Your path to SAP Business Data Cloud

Why Attend

If your organization is still running SAP BW and evaluating modernization, this session delivers the most current practical guidance available — including how AI agents now accelerate the migration journey. Explore proven strategies and dedicated tools that simplify the move to SAP Business Data Cloud while maximizing the value of your existing BW investments.

Key Takeaways

  • Dedicated migration tools and AI agents now automate large portions of the SAP BW modernization journey — reducing manual effort and resource demands while maximizing existing investments.
  • Modernizing to SAP Business Data Cloud isn’t starting over — existing BW models, hierarchies, and business logic are repositioned in a governed, AI-ready data fabric as the foundation for agentic AI, analytics, and planning.
  • Moving to SAP Business Data Cloud is both a technical migration and a strategic upgrade — organizations that modernize now gain a governed, purpose-built agentic AI platform ahead of those still constrained by legacy BW.

 

CT1163 | Under the hood of the Delta Sharing protocol

Why Attend

Zero-copy data sharing is the architectural standard for AI-ready data ecosystems — this technical session gives data engineers the depth to understand and implement the open-source Delta Sharing protocol across cloud and hybrid environments. See how a Delta Sharing server delivers live Delta tables from S3-compatible storage directly to consumers like Databricks — no data movement, no duplication, and governance built in.

Key Takeaways

  • Delta Sharing delivers a zero-copy architecture — live Delta tables stream from S3-compatible storage directly to cloud consumers like Databricks with no duplication, governance and access controls intact.
  • A Delta Sharing server gives engineers practical knowledge to ingest, govern, and operationalize live data sharing between hybrid storage and cloud-native analytics and AI platforms.
  • Together, zero-copy sharing and open standards eliminate two persistent barriers — data movement and proprietary lock-in — giving engineers a replicable, vendor-neutral pattern for connecting distributed data to AI and analytics workloads at scale.

 

Data Analysts

DA105 | Enriching AI models with SAP AI Core in SAP Business Data Cloud

Why Attend

AI models are only as powerful as their business context — this deep dive shows data scientists and practitioners how SAP AI Core integrates with SAP Business Data Cloud to enable semantically enriched, enterprise-grade AI. Learn how to enhance models with rich data products from SAP Business Data Cloud, supporting benchmarking, custom AI development, agentic analytics, and production-ready applications.

Key Takeaways

  • SAP Business Data Cloud data products enrich AI models with business-specific terminology, entity relationships, and domain context — delivering accurate, enterprise-relevant outputs without the overhead of extensive custom training.
  • The session delivers a practical, end-to-end path from governed data to production AI — a clear, repeatable technical approach for agentic analytics practitioners can apply immediately.
  • SAP Business Data Cloud and SAP AI Core carry semantic richness and governance from data products directly into AI model development — closing the gap between trusted enterprise data and reliable, auditable AI outcomes at scale.

 

DA260 | Accelerate agentic planning with trusted data products (hands-on workshop)

Why Attend

The most practical TechEd 2026 session for SAP planning professionals — a 2-hour workshop where you actually build agentic planning workflows, not just hear about them. Work directly with governed data products in SAP Business Data Cloud and SAP Analytics Cloud, learning how agentic AI automates planning tasks, generates insights, and drives faster, more informed decisions.

Key Takeaways

  • SAP Business Data Cloud data products anchor agentic planning to trusted, auditable data — enabling AI agents to automate planning tasks at scale while keeping governance and accountability intact.
  • The hands-on format builds direct SAP Analytics Cloud and SAP Business Data Cloud integration experience — creating business-ready data products and configuring AI workflows that automate repeatable planning activities.
  • Participants leave with end-to-end agentic planning knowledge — from governed data product creation in SAP Business Data Cloud to AI-automated insights and decision support in SAP Analytics Cloud — ready to apply immediately.

 

DA806 | What’s next for agentic analytics and planning in SAP Business Data Cloud

DA806V | What’s next for agentic analytics and planning in SAP Business Data Cloud (virtual)

Why Attend

For SAP Analytics Cloud analysts and planning professionals, this session maps where agentic analytics is heading — what's available now and what's coming — so you can align your strategy ahead of the curve. Discover how Joule Agents are already automating insight delivery, narrative generation, and modeling tasks within SAP Business Data Cloud, transforming analytics and planning into AI-enabled decision engines.

Key Takeaways

  • Joule Agents already automate core analytics workflows — insight delivery, data modeling, and narrative generation — freeing analysts to shift from routine report production to higher-value interpretation and decision support.
  • The session's forward-looking SAP Business Data Cloud roadmap gives practitioners the context to prioritize investments, align architectures, and plan skills development ahead of the curve.
  • Together, today's live capabilities and tomorrow's roadmap give data professionals a complete picture — what to adopt now for immediate productivity gains, and what to prepare for as Joule Agents scale.

 

Data Scientists

ST103 | Behind the Autonomous Enterprise: SAP Knowledge Graph and SAP Domain Models

ST103V | Behind the Autonomous Enterprise: SAP Knowledge Graph and SAP Domain Models (virtual)

entry.title: SAP Business Data Cloud and Datasphere News in September
entry.content:
SAP Business Data Cloud and Datasphere News in September

September closed out Q3 with two releases, seven feature highlights, and one of the most active months the community has seen all year. Data product governance moved from roadmap to reality, replication flows got more complete, and the AI tooling in Datasphere took another step forward.

Learn more in my top features video in September 2026 on YouTube 📺. Also check out the SAP Datasphere Top Features Playlist for all previous months.

In addition, explore the latest updates and blogs in my community news blog.

 

My top features in September

Delta Load for Local Tables (File) as Replication Flow Source

Last month the team added the Initial Only load type for local table file targets. This month they close the gap: delta and initial-plus-delta are now supported too.

You can use local tables stored on object store as a source in a replication flow with both incremental load types. One prerequisite: delta capturing must be enabled on the source table before this will work.

If you have file space pipelines where you want to feed data downstream via a replication flow, the full set of load types is now in place.

➡️  More information

 

 

Transport Runtime Settings for Replication Flows

When you export a replication flow via Transport, you can now choose which runtime settings travel with it: the delta interval, thread limits, email notification configuration, and schema change capture settings. Or all of them at once.

Before this, those settings were not transportable. Every import into a new landscape meant reconfiguring them manually. That step is now gone for teams managing dev, test, and production consistently.

➡️  More information

 

 

Fallback Text for Attribute Translation + Data Validation: Text Entities

Two data modeling improvements that landed in the same release.

First: data validation now supports text entity rules. You can define validation rules that check translation completeness, flag records where expected translations are missing, and surface those as data quality findings. If you're responsible for multi-language model quality, this gives you a proper validation layer where you previously had none.

Second: fallback text for attribute translation. If no translation exists for a given language, you can now specify a fallback text column. So instead of an empty label, users see something meaningful even when coverage isn't complete.

Together these make attribute translation more solid end to end, from catching gaps to handling them gracefully.

➡️  More information

 

 

Data Product Governance Improvements 🚀 Highlight

This one is about trust. A data product economy only works if producers know who's consuming their data and why, and consumers have a clear, consistent path to get access. Without that, you end up with a marketplace where nobody really knows what's being exchanged.

Every data product transaction is now backed by a formal contract. A producer attaches terms and conditions directly to the data product as metadata before any request is submitted. A consumer discovers the data product in the BDC Cockpit or from a Datasphere tenant, sees the terms upfront, and must explicitly accept them before requesting access. They submit a request stating their use case. A data steward reviews and approves or rejects. The outcome is an access agreement: a permanent record of who is consuming what, where, why, and for how long.

This also covers flows that previously happened silently. When you copy a space with data products, install intelligent content, or import an ACN package, a usage agreement is generated automatically.

Auto-approval is a feature, not a shortcut. Data stewards can enable it for low-risk or internal products so consumers get instant access, while the agreement and audit trail are still generated. High-value or sensitive data products go through full review. Producers stay in control without becoming a bottleneck.

The result is a platform where producers are willing to share because they can see how their data is used, and consumers can access what they need because the process is predictable.

➡️  More information

 

 

Object Store Requests Consumed by Category

Object store requests are now metered in three separate categories: Control Plane, Read, and Write. Each has its own per-thousand pricing.

You can see the breakdown in the Capacity Monitor and in Tenant Configuration. Previously you got a single request number. Now you can see exactly which category is driving consumption.

For capacity planning or cost monitoring, this gives you the granularity that was missing before.

➡️  More information

 

 

Add and Clear Filters in Data Integration Monitor ⭐ KP's Pick

My top pick for September: a small UX improvement with a big daily impact.

You can now add column filters directly in the Data Integration Monitor. The active filter conditions are shown in the interface so you can see at a glance what's currently applied. And you can clear them in one step.

If you work in the monitor regularly, you know how much scrolling and state management this replaces.

➡️  More information

 

 

AI SQL Code Generation + Generate Business and Errors & Impacts Summary with AI

Closing with the AI features.

First: AI SQL Code Generation. You can now generate and modify SQL views directly from natural language prompts using SAP Business AI. Describe what you want in plain language, and the system generates the SQL for you. Works in the graphical view editor.

Second: the AI pipeline analyzer has two new capabilities. Business Summary generation gives you an AI-generated description of a pipeline's structure and purpose. Error and Impact analysis surfaces what went wrong in a failed run and what data or processes are affected downstream. Both summaries run against your actual pipeline metadata, so they reflect your specific setup.

If you're managing large numbers of pipelines, the error and impact summary in particular can cut your triage time significantly.

➡️  More information

 

Link to the YouTube video: 

 

SAP Discovery Day for SAP BW Modernization

On October 1, SAP ran a free virtual half-day event for teams thinking about SAP BW modernization. The event was in German.

The program covered modernization paths into SAP Business Data Cloud, customer stories from Zalando and Fresenius, and a roadmap session on where SAP is heading with data and AI. If you missed it, check the event page for recordings or follow-up materials.

Devtoberfest is SAP's annual developer festival, and this year I'm presenting a session on reputation: why it matters for technical professionals, and how to build it without it taking over your life.

The session is on October 6, 14:00–15:00 CEST. Most technical professionals underestimate what reputation actually does for a career. Not the vague personal brand kind. entry.title: S/4HANA to Datasphere: Handling Real-World Data Quality Issues
entry.content:
When moving data from S/4HANA into SAP Datasphere, it is easy to assume that the difficult part is the modeling.

In practice, I found that some of the more time-consuming problems appeared before the modeling logic became the problem at all.

We were working on an analytics project where S/4HANA data was being brought into Datasphere and then exposed for SAP Analytics Cloud reporting. The overall architecture was straightforward: bring the required source data into Datasphere, build the transformation and semantic layers, and consume the resulting models in SAC.

What made the work interesting was what happened when we started looking closely at the data.

A field could exist in S/4HANA, be available in the source view, appear in Datasphere, and still not behave the way we expected once it was used in a model. That changed the way I approached data quality. I stopped treating it as something to check after the model was built. It became part of the modeling process itself.

Data availability does not mean data readiness

One of the first assumptions I had to challenge was: "If the field exists in the S/4HANA source, it should be ready for reporting."

That isn't necessarily true.

A field can be technically available but still create problems for the analytical model. In the project, the issues generally fell into three areas:

Technical issues

  • Data types and invalid values
  • Replication constraints
  • Missing or incomplete source records

Structural issues

  • Joins changing the expected population
  • Unexpected aggregation behaviour
  • Differences between source views and underlying data

Semantic issues

  • GL account mappings
  • Master-data relationships
  • Business classifications that did not align with the transactional population

This becomes particularly important when the data is consumed through several layers.

For example:
S4/HANA → Replication/Ingestion → Local Table → Integration/Harmonization → Reporting Model → SAC

A problem introduced at the source can therefore become visible several layers later. By the time the SAC chart shows an unexpected number, the actual cause may be several transformations away. That was one of the first lessons I took from the project.

The source view is not always the source of truth

One of the issues we encountered involved a CDS-based source that looked suitable for replication.

The view exposed the business fields required for the reporting requirement, so from a functional perspective it looked like the right starting point. The problem appeared when we checked the technical requirements for the Replication Flow.

The CDS view did not provide key fields required for the replication approach we were using. That meant that although the view was useful from a business and semantic perspective, it was not suitable as a direct replication source.

This was one of those issues that is easy to discover late if the focus is only on the fields exposed by the source.

We therefore had to look one layer deeper and identify the underlying data structure that could support the required replication approach.

Instead of asking: "Which CDS view contains the field I need?"
We started asking: "What is the actual persistence and replication requirement behind this field?"

That led us toward the underlying local/raw data structure instead.

This distinction is important because a source object can be perfectly valid from an application or semantic perspective and still not be the right object for a particular data integration pattern.

In other words:
Business-readable source ≠ automatically replication-ready source

That is something I would now check much earlier in a Datasphere implementation.

A field existing in two places does not mean the two fields are equivalent

Another issue appeared when working with GL account information and semantic tagging.

In the project, we were using a semantic-tagging structure containing roughly 1,500 GL account entries to support the financial reporting logic. At the same time, the underlying financial transactional data contained a much larger population of around 20 lakh records.

At first, it was tempting to assume that the semantic-tagging table represented the complete population that should exist in the transactional data.

When we started reconciling the two, that assumption did not hold.

The accounts available in the semantic-tagging structure did not fully correspond to the accounts appearing in the transactional population. We also had to consider the chart of accounts being used in the reporting scope rather than treating every tagged account as universally applicable.

That changed the nature of the investigation.

At that point, the question was no longer: "Why doesn't my join work?"
The better question was: "Are these two datasets actually describing the same business population?"

That distinction matters.

A mapping or semantic table can contain valid business definitions that are broader than the current transactional dataset.

It may contain:

  • accounts not currently used
  • accounts belonging to another scope
  • accounts from another chart of accounts
  • historical values
  • values maintained for future reporting requirements

So seeing an account in a semantic table does not prove that the account should appear in the fact data. The join itself was not necessarily wrong.

Our assumption about the relationship between the datasets was what needed to be investigated.

The zero-value problem that looked like a calculation issue

The most interesting example came from financial measures.

We were working with an amount measure from the financial transaction data. The requirement was to present certain financial values using the reporting sign expected by the business.

We created an inverted amount measure.

The expectation was straightforward: Source amount - invert the sign as a positive reporting value where required. Instead, the resulting measure was showing zero in the analytical output.

Initially, this looked like a calculation problem.

Was the inversion expression wrong?
Was the aggregation wrong?
Was SAC interpreting the measure incorrectly?

But when we went back to the underlying data, the situation became clearer. The issue was not simply the inversion.

The underlying financial data contained positive and negative postings whose aggregation behavior needed to be understood before applying the reporting transformation.

In other words, we were trying to solve a business-sign problem at the measure level before fully understanding the accounting behavior of the underlying records.

That was an important distinction.

A calculated measure can be technically correct and still produce an unexpected business result if the assumptions about the source data are wrong.

Don't debug the final measure first

This experience changed the way I troubleshoot Datasphere models.

When an SAC KPI or chart shows an unexpected value, my first instinct now is not to modify the SAC calculation. I work backwards.

  1. What does the SAC widget actually receive?
    Is the problem already present in the analytical model?
  2. What does the analytical model return?
    If the value is already wrong here, SAC is probably not the root cause.

  3. What does the underlying fact view contain?
    Check the actual records before aggregation.

  4. What did the harmonization layer do?
    Look for joins, filters, calculated columns, and semantic restrictions.

  5. What was actually replicated?
    Finally, go back to the raw/local table and compare it with the source.

The flow becomes:
SAC result → Analytical Model → Fact View → Harmonization View → Local Table → S4/HANA Source

This sounds obvious, but it saves a surprising amount of time. If the value is already incorrect in the fact view, changing the SAC story is unlikely to solve anything.

Data quality is also about semantics

Another lesson was that data quality isn't limited to things such as nulls, invalid dates, or duplicate records. There is another category that is much harder to detect: semantic correctness.

A value can be:

  • populated
  • correctly typed
  • successfully replicated
  • successfully joined

and still be wrong for the business meaning we are trying to represent. The GL account example made this particularly clear. The account value itself could be perfectly valid. The problem was whether it represented the same reporting meaning as the account we were trying to map it to.

The same principle applies to:

  • Company Code
  • Sales Organization
  • Customer
  • Material
  • Currency
  • Fiscal Period
  • Cost Center
  • GL Account

A technically valid join does not automatically mean a semantically valid relationship. 

This is why I increasingly think of data quality in Datasphere in three layers:
Technical quality → Can the data be loaded and queried? → Structural quality → Does the data model relate correctly? → Semantic quality → Does the data mean what the business thinks it means?

All three need to be validated.

When the data looks correct, but the model is wrong

There was another class of issue that initially pointed us toward the source data but eventually turned out to be related to the model.

For example, a source dataset could contain the expected records, but after introducing a join or restriction in a graphical view, the resulting dataset could change significantly. This is where row-level validation becomes useful.

Suppose the raw layer contains:
200,000 records

After a transformation:
198,500 records

That difference is not automatically a problem. But it should be explainable.

Were 1,500 records intentionally filtered?
Did a join remove unmatched records?
Did a condition exclude null values?
Did the semantic mapping only cover part of the population?
Or was the relationship itself incorrect?

A model should not simply produce a number. The change in population between layers should have a reason.

The importance of checking the intermediate layer

One of the practices I found particularly useful was validating intermediate outputs instead of waiting until the final analytical model.

For example:

LayerWhat I should validate
RawRecord availability and source values
HarmonizationJoins, mappings, and transformations
Reporting Measures, aggregation, and business rules
SACFilters, dimensions, and visual output

This gives each layer a responsibility. If something changes between two layers, we know where to investigate. Without that separation, debugging becomes much more difficult because the final result contains the combined effect of everything that happened before it.

Data quality issues are often architecture issues in disguise

One of the broader lessons from this work is that a data problem is not always solved by cleaning the data. Sometimes the problem is where we decided to implement something.

For example:

  • A mapping embedded in a calculation may belong in a reference table.
  • A source field that cannot be reliably replicated may require a different ingestion approach.
  • A business classification may belong in the semantic layer rather than the SAC story.
  • A sign transformation may require a clearer definition of the underlying accounting behavior.
  • A missing relationship may indicate that the master-data model needs to be reconsidered.

This is why I don't see data quality and architecture as completely separate topics. The way we model data affects the way we can detect and explain quality issues.

What I would check earlier next time

After working through these issues, I would add a few checks much earlier in the project.

Validate the source before designing the model

Don't start with the target SAC chart. Start by understanding the source population.

Check replication suitability early

A source view may expose the right business fields but still not satisfy the requirements of the chosen replication mechanism.

Profile critical fields

For fields such as GL Account, Company Code, Currency, and dates, understand the actual values before building dependent logic.

Validate mappings independently

Don't wait for a final reporting number to tell you that two mapping structures don't align. Check the mapping population separately.

Reconcile record counts between layers

Whenever records disappear or multiply, know why.

Validate measures before building the story

A KPI should already be trusted at the model level before it becomes a polished SAC tile. 

These checks don't necessarily require a large additional process. They simply move validation earlier, when fixing a problem is cheaper.

The bigger lesson

Working with S/4HANA data in Datasphere changed my understanding of what "data quality" means in an analytics project.

Initially, I thought of data quality mostly as a source-data problem. After working through the implementation, I see it differently.

There are at least three questions we need to answer:

  • Is the data technically valid?
  • Is it structurally correct for the model?
  • Does it represent the business meaning we think it represents?

The third question is usually the hardest. 
A Datasphere model can activate successfully.
The replication can complete successfully.
The SAC story can display successfully.
And the result can still be wrong.

That is why I now prefer to trace an unexpected number all the way back through the model instead of trying to fix the final output immediately.

The most useful question is often not: "Why is this number wrong?"
It is: "At which layer did this number stop representing what the business intended?"

Once that question becomes part of the development process, troubleshooting becomes less about trial and error and more about understanding how the data moved through the architecture.

For me, that has been one of the more valuable lessons from working with S/4HANA data in SAP Datasphere.

entry.title: Why Your SAP Datasphere Measure Shows 0 Even When the Source Has Millions of Records ?
entry.content:
A common issue in SAP Datasphere Finance models is a measure returning 0 even though the underlying S/4HANA source contains millions of records with valid amounts.

This can be particularly confusing when the data is successfully available in the source, and the Datasphere model itself is technically valid.

The important point is:
A valid source dataset does not guarantee a valid analytical measure.

The complete data path must be validated:
S/4HANA CDS → Replication Flow → RAW → Harmonization/Foundation → Semantic Logic → Analytical Model → SAC

1. Validate the replication source first

The first validation should not be the SAC story or the Analytical Model. Start with the source and replication layer. A CDS view returning data from S/4HANA does not automatically mean that it is suitable for replication through a Datasphere Replication Flow.

One critical validation is the availability of appropriate key fields. Replication requires a reliable mechanism to identify records and, depending on the replication scenario, support initial and subsequent data processing.

Therefore, validate:

  • Is the CDS view supported for the selected replication mechanism?
  • Are the required key fields exposed?
  • Is the source suitable for the required initial/delta replication behavior?
  • Are there replication-flow errors or warnings?
  • Is the expected number of records reaching the target?
  • Does the target RAW table contain the expected amount of values?

This distinction is important:
CDS view returns data ≠ Replication source is correctly configured ≠ RAW contains the expected analytical dataset

A source can contain millions of records while the downstream model is working with an incomplete or unsuitable dataset.

2. Reconcile the data layer by layer

The fastest way to isolate the issue is to reconcile the measure at every layer.

LayerValidation
S/4HANA / CDSRecord count and source amount
Replication FlowLoad status, errors, record processing
RAWRecord count and amount
Foundation / HarmonizationFilters, joins, and transformations
Analytical ModelMeasures and aggregation
SACFilters, dimensions, and visualization aggregation

For example:

Source → Expected records: X, Expected amount: Y
↓
RAW → Records: X?, Amount: Y?
↓
Foundation View → Records: X?, Amount: Y?
↓
Analytical Model → Amount: Y?
↓
SAC → Amount: Y?

The first layer where Y changes or becomes 0 is the layer that requires investigation.

3. Validate the base measure before applying restrictions

For Finance scenarios, the base measure may be something such as:

Amount in Global Currency

Before creating restricted measures such as COGS, Revenue, or other GL-account-based measures, validate the unrestricted amount.

The validation sequence should be:
Amount in Global Currency → Aggregation → Semantic classification → GL Account restriction → Sign/inversion logic → Restricted Measure

Do not validate all of these simultaneously. If the unrestricted amount itself returns 0, investigating the COGS or Revenue restriction will not solve the underlying problem.

4. Check semantic classification and restrictions

Finance models often use semantic information to classify accounts and create reusable measures.

For example:
GL Account → Semantic Classification → Account Category → Restricted Measure

If the restriction is based on a semantic classification, validate the classification independently.

A useful diagnostic is to compare:
Total Amount vs. Amount for classified accounts vs. Amount for restricted measure

If the total amount is populated but the restricted measure is 0, the issue is no longer the replication volume. The investigation should move to:

  • GL account mapping

  • semantic tags/classification
  • restriction conditions
  • company code/context
  • sign handling
  • aggregation behavior

5. Validate sign and inversion logic

Finance reporting introduces another common source of confusion: sign conventions. 

A source amount may already contain accounting signs, while the reporting requirement may expect the opposite presentation.

For example:
Source amount is -100,000
Reporting requirement is 100,000

An inverted measure may therefore be appropriate. However, inversion should be validated only after confirming that the underlying population is correct.

The following two situations are fundamentally different:
Correct records + incorrect sign and Incorrect/empty restricted population

Both can produce an unexpected result, but they require completely different fixes.

6. Validate the fact-table grain

A second major area is data grain.

A Finance fact record may exist at a much more detailed level than the reporting requirement:
Company Code + Fiscal Year + Fiscal Period + Document + GL Account + Cost Center + Profit Center + ...

When additional dimensions or master-data joins are introduced, the cardinality of those joins must be validated.

A non-unique join can transform:
1 fact record → multiple joined records

and subsequently produce incorrect aggregation.

Therefore, record counts should be checked not only after replication, but also after major joins and transformations.

7. A practical diagnostic sequence

For a measure returning 0, the following sequence provides a reliable isolation path:

  1. Validate source CDS data
  2. Validate CDS replication compatibility
  3. Validate key fields
  4. Validate Replication Flow execution
  5. Validate RAW record count
  6. Validate RAW amount
  7. Validate fact-table grain
  8. Validate joins and cardinality
  9. Validate unrestricted measure
  10. Validate semantic classification
  11. Validate restricted measure
  12. Validate sign/inversion
  13. Validate Analytical Model aggregation
  14. Validate SAC filters and aggregation

This prevents the common mistake of modifying SAC calculations when the actual problem exists in the ingestion or modeling layer.

Key takeaway

For SAP Datasphere analytical models, “the source contains data” is only the first validation point.

A reliable measure depends on the entire chain:

Source validity → Replication compatibility → Data completeness → Correct grain → Correct transformations → Semantic classification → Measure definition → Aggregation → Consumption

When a measure returns 0, the correct question is not simply: “Why is SAC showing zero?”
The better question is: “At which layer does the expected value stop being represented correctly?”

That distinction significantly reduces the troubleshooting scope and is especially important for Finance models built on replicated S/4HANA data.

entry.title: Managing the Custom Data Product Lifecycle in SAP Datasphere / SAP BDC
entry.content:
If you are publishing Custom Data Products / Data Products in the Data Sharing Cockpit of SAP Datasphere / SAP BDC, creating the product is only half the story. The other half is what happens next — listing it, versioning it, updating its artifacts, and eventually retiring it.

On the surface, a data product looks like a one-time deliverable. In practice, it has a full lifecycle, and every status change carries rules about what you can and cannot do next.

This matters most if you build your own custom data products in SAP Business Data Cloud. On a Delta Share runtime, you create them in SAP Datasphere and manage them from the My Data Products page — found under Utilities → Data Sharing Cockpit → My Data Products (it is a page in the Data Sharing Cockpit, not a standalone app). Every lifecycle rule below applies directly to them.

First, know which kind of data product you have. A product’s behaviour depends on its Context:

 Formation (BDC custom)Public Data Marketplace
ContextFormationsPublic Data Marketplace
Delivery ModeDelta ShareFull Replication / One Time Replication / Live Access
VisibilityUnified Customer LandscapePublic
Licenses / pricingNoneYes (contract types, licenses)
Deactivate & Usage OverviewNot availableAvailable

This blog follows the Formation track — the custom data products you build for SAP Business Data Cloud. Where a step behaves differently for Public Data Marketplace products, you will see a “Marketplace products differ” note.

 

1. What Are the Lifecycle Statuses of a Data Product?

Every custom data product moves through a defined set of statuses, shown in the system as its Lifecycle Status. You control most of them from the My Data Products page via the Switch Status button. Here is what each one means:

StatusWhat It Means
DraftThe initial state right after creation. Not yet visible in the Catalog & Marketplace.
ListingA transient state while the product is being listed — typically 2–5 minutes. Switch Status and Edit are locked until it finishes.
ListedLive and discoverable in the Catalog & Marketplace.
DelistedRemoved from the pool of available products — but existing consumers keep access, and you can still create new releases. A failed listing attempt shows as “Delisted (Listing Failed)”.
DeletedPhysically removed as far as possible. Terminal — and the technical name can never be reused.
BlockedOnly SAP can set this — for non-compliance or disputes. It overlays your status without changing it, and reverts once SAP lifts the block.

Marketplace products differ: Public Data Marketplace products add a Deactivated status (no new releases or licenses; existing licenses can still be changed; choose List to re-activate). Formation data products do not have it — they have no licenses to deactivate.

Marketplace products differ (Usage Overview): On a Public Data Marketplace product’s details page you also get a Usage Overview tab showing active/expired licenses, recent activations, and recent updates — and it will stop you from deleting a product that still has active licenses. Formation products do not expose a Usage Overview tab.

2. Which Status Transitions Are Actually Allowed?

Not every status can jump to every other status. For a Formation data product the headline rules are:

  • Draft → can be Listed, or Deleted.
  • Listed → can only be Delisted (and Blocked by SAP).
  • Delisted → can go back to Listed, or be Deleted.
  • Deleted → terminal. And you cannot reuse that product’s technical name afterward.

Two things that trip people up:

  • Delete is its own button, not a Switch Status option. Switch Status only offers List / Delist; deleting is the separate Delete (or Delete Product) button.
  • A live product cannot be deleted directly. While a product is Listed the Delete button is disabled — you delist it first, then delete. Plan the exit, don’t improvise it.

Marketplace products differ: a delisted Public Data Marketplace product can also be Deactivated (Switch Status then offers List + Deactivate). A delisted Formation product offers only List — there is no Deactivate.

 

3. How Does Versioning Communicate Change to Consumers?

Data products use three-number semantic versioning — [ Major . Minor . Patch ] — so consumers instantly understand the impact of an update.

LevelCompatibilityWhat It Covers
Major (X.0.0)IncompatibleBreaking changes — e.g. removing a table or columns. Not supported: you must create a new product instead.
Minor (1.X.0)CompatibleBackward-compatible additions — new tables, a new column, a renamed column. Existing integrations keep working.
Patch (1.0.X)CompatibleBug fixes and maintenance. Currently not applied to data products.

The key rule to internalize: you can add to a listed data product, but you cannot take away. Adding a table or column bumps the minor version automatically (in testing, adding one table moved a product from 1.1.0 → 1.2.0). Removing content is a breaking change — and that means a brand-new product.

4. How Do You Update Artifacts on an Already-Listed Product?

For products on a Delta Share runtime in an SAP Business Data Cloud formation, you can extend a live product without taking it down. Open My Data Products → select the product → Edit Product, then go to the Product Artifacts section:

  • Use Add Artifacts to add tables, or add columns to an existing artifact to pull in newly created fields.
  • Click Save. The product status becomes “Changes to List”; use Switch Status → List to publish the update. The minor version updates automatically.

Two things worth remembering:

  • Add only — you cannot remove. Per SAP documentation you can only add elements to a listed product; removing a table or column that is already part of a listed product is a breaking change and is not supported. (The editor does show a Delete Artifacts button, but that is for artifacts you have added and not yet listed.)
  • If you delist the product before re-listing it, any newly added artifacts are silently removed.

5. When — and How — Can You Delete a Data Product?

Deletion uses the separate Delete button and is gated by status. For a Formation product you can delete when it is in Draft or Delisted and has no active installations; while it is Listed the Delete button is disabled.

Deleting asks you to confirm, and the warning is blunt:

“Are you sure you want to delete the data product permanently? Once deleted, data products cannot be restored. You cannot create a data product with the same technical name anymore.”

So the hard stops are: the technical name is burned forever once deleted, and if consumers already activated the product, delivery-tracking and transaction history stay in the system so those consumers keep their full history.

Watch out when the product is shared externally: delisting a product that is still shared with external systems raises a warning (“…still shared with external systems in the catalog… consider unsharing this data product in the catalog first”). Stop the share before you delist.

Marketplace products differ: Public Data Marketplace products add license-based delete rules — e.g. you cannot delete a product with active licenses; a Free product with active installations or one whose license expired more than 90 days ago (and was never activated) can be deleted. These rules do not apply to Formation products, which have no licenses.

6. What You See in the SAP BDC Catalog

The statuses above are the provider view, in the SAP Datasphere Data Sharing Cockpit. The consumer side speaks a different language. In the SAP BDC cockpit (and the Catalog & Marketplace), the same product shows a Lifecycle Status of Active or Inactive — plus a separate Release Status. So a product you Listed appears as Active in the catalog; one you Deactivated (Marketplace) appears as Inactive. Deactivate is actioned in the provider cockpit; the catalog only reflects the result.

7. Takeaway

Think of a custom data product’s lifecycle like publishing a book. Draft is your manuscript — private, freely editable. Listing puts it on the shelf for readers. A minor version is a new printing with extra chapters added — everyone’s existing copy still reads fine. A major change isn’t an edit at all; it’s a different book with a new title. And delisting and deleting are how you take it out of print — gently for existing readers, permanently for the catalog.

The golden rules that keep you out of trouble: add, never remove; delist (and unshare) before you delete; and remember a deleted technical name never comes back. Know whether you are working with a Formation or a Public Data Marketplace product, and the Data Sharing Cockpit becomes a very predictable place to work.

entry.title: Did You Know? An SAP Business Data Cloud Series | Season 1, Episode 2 | Translation
entry.content:
The Problem Hidden in Plain Sight 

Global organizations run on shared understanding. When a finance team in Munich, a supply chain group in Tokyo, and a sales operation in São Paulo all rely on the same analytics, the data needs to speak each audience's language... literally! Column headers in English, dimension labels nobody recognizes, and master data descriptions stripped of local context create friction that slows adoption and quietly erodes trust in the numbers. 

Differing languages can become a barrier between good data and confident decision-making. When people cannot immediately understand what they are looking at, they second-guess the insight, ask for clarification, or build their own workaround reports. None of those outcomes serve the business well. 

Well, here’s the kicker: the fix is already in SAP Datasphere! It's called Translation, a feature that comes included in your solution. There's a chance your team hasn't fully explored it yet, and the effort to get started is lower than most people expect. 

What Is Translation in SAP Datasphere? 

Translation in SAP Datasphere is what it sounds like: a tool to help translate your data. More specifically, it’s a multilingual support capability with two complementary layers: metadata translation and master data translation. Together, they allow the same analytic model and SAP Analytics Cloud story to be consumed by users in their own language without duplicating your models or building separate environments per region. 

Think of it as making your data infrastructure genuinely multilingual. Labels, column names, dimension descriptions, and the actual data values that appear inside charts and tables can all reflect the language of the person viewing them. The underlying model stays the same. Only the rendered experience changes. 

Furthermore, both metadata and master data layers are designed to be managed without custom development. If your organization is global and your analytics are currently single-language, the translation feature closes that gap in a way that's governed, maintainable, and built into the platform you already have. 

Layer 1: Metadata Translation 

The Translation Dashboard is the central workspace for translating the structural labels of data models: business names, column names on dimensions and analytic models, and hierarchy labels consumed in SAP Analytics Cloud stories. These are the elements that describe the data rather than the data itself. 

The workflow is straightforward. Once translation is enabled for a space and a source language is set, users select the objects they want to translate and choose between two options: translating manually within the dashboard, or exporting content as an XLIFF file, the industry-standard format used by professional translation tools, sending it for translation, and importing the translated file back in. Multiple target languages, multiple XLIFF files, one centrally managed dashboard. Users with the Translation privilege in their scoped role can create, review, and manage translations from a single location. 

This approach integrates translation into the modelling lifecycle rather than treating it as a separate project. Teams can translate incrementally - starting with the most widely consumed analytic models and expanding coverage as regional adoption grows. 

Layer 2: Master Data Translation 

Metadata translation handles labels. But what about the actual data values: the product names, customer descriptions, cost center names that appear inside your charts and tables? 

That's where master data translation comes in. You model a Text entity in Datasphere, a table with Semantic Usage set to Text, that holds language-specific descriptions for your master data, then create a text association linking your dimension to it. When a user views the model with their Data Access Language set to French, they see French descriptions. Set it to Japanese, they see Japanese. The model doesn't change- only what's rendered for each user does! 

This is especially powerful for SAP customers because master data in S/4HANA often already carries multilingual text tables. Datasphere is designed to carry that linguistic richness forward into your analytics layer, rather than setting everything to a single language at extraction. 

Translation in Action

Watch this video for a quick demonstration of how Translation works in SAP Datasphere!

 

Try It Yourself! 

Translation is available today in SAP Datasphere as part of your SAP Business Data Cloud subscription. Start by enabling translation for one of your Spaces, pick an analytic model your team uses regularly, and run through the Translation Dashboard for a single target language. The experience of seeing a familiar model rendered in a second language is often the catalyst that drives broader adoption. 

If your master data already has language-dependent text tables in your source system, check whether those text associations have been modelled in Datasphere. You may find multilingual support is closer to ready than you think. 

Have you already set up multilingual models in your BDC environment? Share how you approached it in the comments below. 

 

Next up in Season 1, Episode 3, we’ll explore Joule for Datasphere!

entry.title: Managing Parent-Child Hierarchies in SAC: One Small Update That Simplifies Everything
entry.content:
Introduction

Every once in a while SAP delivers a feature that doesn't make it into keynotes or release highlights. Yet some of these smaller improvements can have a surprisingly large impact on day-to-day development.

One such improvement recently appeared in SAC hierarchy loading. While it may look like a minor technical change, it removes one of the reasons why hierarchy loads often required additional preprocessing, filtering logic, and cleanup workarounds.

 

The Old Behavior

Imagine your dimension has members, that are not completely assigned to the hierarchy. In this example, there are Marketing CostCenters assigned to a Marketing Node, while the Production (P_...) CostCenters are not assigned to the hierarchy:

 

Member IDParent
M_AMarketing
M_BMarketing
M_CMarketing
P_ANULL
P_BNULL
P_CNULL
Marketing 

With the traditional SAC load behavior, members without a parent assignment were automatically placed below <root>.

As a result, the loaded hierarchy looked like this:

This behavior was often undesirable.

The Production cost centers were valid dimension members, but they were not intended to be part of the Marketing hierarchy. Nevertheless, SAC automatically added them as root nodes because no parent assignment was provided.

For dimensions with multiple hierarchies, this quickly became a challenge. Every hierarchy would suddenly contain large numbers of unrelated members below <root>, making the hierarchy difficult to maintain and more difficult for business users to navigate.

Because of this, a common recommendation emerged:

  1. Load all dimension members first.
  2. Load each hierarchy separately.
  3. Restrict every hierarchy load to the members that actually belong to that hierarchy.

While effective, this approach introduced additional data flows, transformations, and maintenance effort solely to avoid unwanted <root> assignments.

 

The New Behavior

Now SAC can distinguish between three fundamentally different scenarios:

  • assigned to a parent node
  • assigned to <root>  (blank / empty string)
  • not assigned to the hierarchy (NULL )

Using the same example, the hierarchy load can now provide NULL for members that should be excluded from the hierarchy:

The Production cost centers remain valid dimension members, but they are no longer added to the hierarchy:

This seemingly small change eliminates one of the main reasons why hierarchies had to be loaded separately in the first place.

If you are using Seamless Planning with Datasphere or expose SAC master data through the Data Provisioning Agent (DPA), this enhancement becomes even more valuable.

Instead of maintaining hierarchy assignments separately, you can use the existing dimension members as the starting point and simply join them with the hierarchy source. Members without a matching hierarchy assignment can be loaded with a NULL parent value and are automatically removed from the hierarchy:

SQL Example: Exposed Dimension Members in Datasphere with Hierarchy Join

This makes it much easier to keep hierarchies synchronized with the actual set of active members and to clean up obsolete hierarchy assignments. 

For the first time, hierarchy loads can be used not only to create or change hierarchy relationships, but also to remove them!

 

Impact on Existing Hierarchy Workarounds

In my previous blog post, I described one of the key limitations of SAC hierarchy loading: members could not truly leave a hierarchy through the load process. When a parent assignment was cleared, SAC interpreted the record as a root member and placed it below <root> instead.

However, this limitation had implications far beyond hierarchy cleanup.

Because SAC treated missing parent assignments as <root>, a common recommendation emerged for dimensions with multiple hierarchies: load the master data first and maintain each hierarchy separately. Otherwise, members that did not belong to a specific hierarchy would still appear in that hierarchy as root nodes.

As a consequence, additional filtering logic, separate hierarchy loads, and custom cleanup procedures became common implementation patterns.

With the new NULL handling, many of these workarounds are no longer required.

A NULL parent assignment now explicitly removes the hierarchy relationship while keeping the member itself in the dimension. Members that do not belong to a hierarchy no longer have to be excluded from the load process entirely. Instead, they can simply be loaded with a NULL parent value.

The benefit is especially visible when using Seamless Planning or exposing SAC dimensions through the Data Provisioning Agent (DPA). In these scenarios, existing SAC members can be used as the starting point, joined with the hierarchy source, and loaded back into SAC. Members without a matching hierarchy assignment simply receive a NULL parent value and are removed from the hierarchy automatically.

 

Conclusion

For many years, the behavior of SAC hierarchy loads shaped common implementation practices. Separate hierarchy loads, additional filtering logic, and hierarchy cleanup workarounds were often necessary to avoid unwanted <root> assignments.

With the introduction of NULL-based hierarchy removal, SAC now provides a clear distinction between:

  • a member assigned to a parent node
  • a member assigned to <root>
  • a member that does not belong to the hierarchy at all

This seemingly small enhancement not only solves one of the limitations discussed in my previous blog post. It also simplifies the loading of dimensions with multiple hierarchies and reduces the need for several long-standing implementation workarounds.

No keynote. No release highlight. Just a small change that quietly removes one of the longest-standing pain points in SAC hierarchy loading.
