entry.title: SAP Datasphere Replication Flow Fails with CDS Views Having No Key Fields — What Actually Happens?
entry.content:
A CDS view can return valid data in SAP S/4HANA and still be unsuitable for a particular replication scenario in SAP Datasphere.

One issue I encountered while working with Finance data was a CDS source that did not expose the required key fields for replication. The source data was available, but the replication approach had constraints that needed to be addressed before the data could be consumed downstream.

Understanding the role of keys is essential to diagnosing this correctly.

1. Why does a Replication Flow require key fields?

A primary key uniquely identifies a record within a dataset. In replication scenarios, this identity becomes particularly important when the source supports inserts, updates, and deletes.

Consider the following source data:

Company CodeDocumentLine ItemAmount
1000190000010015,000
1000190000010023,000
1000190000020017,000

If the document number alone is treated as the key, the first two records cannot be uniquely identified. A suitable key might require a combination of company code, document number, fiscal year, and line item, depending on the source object's actual business grain.

Without a reliable record identity, the replication mechanism cannot safely apply record-level changes using an arbitrary key.

SAP documents this limitation in KBA 3531135.

2. What happens when the CDS view has no key?

When adding a source object to a Replication Flow, you may encounter an error similar to:

The following source objects are not supported because they do not have a primary key.

However, a missing primary key does not automatically mean that every replication scenario is unsupported.

SAP Datasphere supports certain CDS views and ODP source objects without primary keys under documented conditions. These sources are restricted to Initial Only loading in the applicable scenarios; Initial and Delta processing is not supported without the required key definition. See SAP KBA 3543361.

The distinction is important:

  • Initial Only: Loads the source data for that run without ongoing delta replication.

  • Initial and Delta: Performs the initial load and subsequently replicates supported changes.

  • Delta Only: Replicates subsequent changes without performing an initial full load.

The available options depend on the source connection, source object type, and extraction capabilities. A CDS view must also meet the relevant extraction prerequisites.

3. How should the issue be diagnosed?

Before changing the data model, validate the source and connection configuration.

Step 1: Verify the CDS definition

Inspect the CDS view's key fields and extraction annotations. Confirm that the view is supported for the intended replication scenario.

For ABAP CDS sources, delta-enabled extraction commonly requires appropriate @analytics.dataExtraction annotations, including change-data-capture configuration where applicable.

Step 2: Verify the connection type

The key definition visible through the ABAP Dictionary may differ from the definition exposed at the HANA database layer.

For example, SAP's documentation describes cases involving tables such as ACDOCA, where a key exists in the ABAP application dictionary but not at the HANA database layer. The selected connection type can therefore affect source-object validation.

See SAP KBA 3531135.

Step 3: Check the required load type

Determine whether the requirement is a one-time snapshot or ongoing synchronization.

If the source has no primary key and meets the documented prerequisites, Initial Only may be an option. If ongoing delta replication is mandatory, the source design or extraction approach may need to change.

4. What are the practical alternatives?

The correct solution depends on the source and business requirement.

  • Use Initial Only: Suitable when a one-time snapshot is sufficient, and the source meets SAP's prerequisites.

  • Use an appropriate extraction-enabled CDS view: Prefer a supported source that exposes the required key and delta semantics.

  • Use an appropriate ODP extractor: Consider an existing supported extractor when it provides the required business data and extraction behavior.

  • Use SLT where appropriate: For supported table-replication scenarios, configure the source table for SLT replication and consume it through the supported connection and container.

  • Redesign the source: If a custom CDS view is involved, review its grain, key definition, and extraction capabilities before using it as a replication source.

Do not introduce an arbitrary key merely to bypass validation. A concatenated or generated key is safe only if it is stable, unique at the actual record grain, and compatible with the replication mechanism. It does not, by itself, enable delta extraction.

5. Key takeaway

A CDS view being queryable does not guarantee that it is suitable for replication. The source must satisfy the extraction, key, and load-type requirements of the selected Replication Flow scenario.

Before troubleshooting downstream Datasphere views, validate the source object's replication compatibility first. This prevents modeling work from being built on an ingestion approach that cannot meet the required data consistency or refresh requirements.

Reference: SAP Help Portal — Select Source and Target Connections for Replication Flows

entry.title: SAP S/4HANA Group Reporting and SAP BDC: Why Replacing SEM-BCS Is More Than a Tool Change
entry.content:
For companies using SAP SEM-BCS, the end of maintenance for standard SAP BW is more than a system issue. They need to reorganize consolidation and their data architecture so that group financial statements, group planning, and corporate reporting as a whole continue to be based on consistent figures.

This article explains why Group Reporting is not merely a technical replacement, what roles SAP Datasphere and SAP BDC play in integrated corporate reporting, and what the business and IT teams should examine before making an architectural decision.

SAP’s Target Architecture: Group Reporting on a Common Data Foundation

Standard SAP BW is no longer at the center of SAP’s target architecture. SEM-BCS users therefore need both a new consolidation solution and a perspective for their BW-based data and reporting landscape.

SAP S/4HANA for Group Reporting handles consolidation, while SAP BDC exchanges master and transaction data between Enterprise Performance Management (EPM) applications, meaning solutions for consolidation, planning, reporting, and analysis. Only this connection turns the system change into integrated corporate reporting.

S/4HANA for Group Reporting: Consolidation Closer to Operational Finance

SAP S/4HANA for Group Reporting supports a wide range of group structures and consolidation scenarios with currency translation, intercompany eliminations, validations, journal entries, approvals, and audit trails. Its key advantage over an isolated solution is its proximity to operational FI/CO data.

Stand-Alone or ERP-Integrated: Two Paths for Consolidation

Group Reporting can run as stand-alone consolidation in a dedicated S/4HANA system or be integrated into the central S/4HANA system. Additional reported data can be incorporated via SAP Group Reporting Data Collection using forms, file uploads, APIs, or OData—including from non-SAP systems or for non-financial disclosures.

The decisive factor is how closely consolidation and operational accounting need to work together. The integrated option reduces system breaks in centralized S/4HANA landscapes; the stand-alone model offers greater flexibility with multiple ERP systems or separate responsibilities.

SAP Business Data Cloud Becomes the Integration Layer in Corporate Reporting

SAP BDC forms the data foundation of the EPM architecture. It combines data lake and data warehouse functions, exchanges master and transaction data between Group Reporting, SAP Analytics Cloud Planning, and other applications, and creates the basis for reports and dashboards.

 

For groups with multiple S/4HANA instances, the planned BDC data transfer layer is particularly relevant: It is intended to take transaction data from public- and private-cloud systems and transform it according to central rules. Mapping, derivation, substitution, and aggregation are performed in a controlled manner; the original data is retained.

This keeps transformations traceable and the origin of the figures visible. Large volumes of data can be processed in near real time; at the same time, this creates the foundation for continuous intercompany reconciliation at account level.

Data Products Provide Access—the Complete Reporting Logic Is Emerging Step by Step

Group Reporting content for master data and raw transaction data is already available for SAP Datasphere. Companies can use it to build their own models and reports. However, reporting items, rules, and the complete Group Reporting logic are not yet consistently covered as SAP-managed content in the BDC target architecture.

Companies therefore need to determine early on where the reporting logic resides, which models they will manage themselves in Datasphere, and which can later be supplemented by SAP content. Otherwise, old dependencies will simply migrate to a new platform.

 

 

New Functions Address Bottlenecks in the Financial Close Process

The functions introduced or announced for 2025 and 2026 address typical bottlenecks in the group financial close: Validations check reported data that has not yet been released, a Fiori app supports imports, prior periods can be reopened for release, and the consolidation monitor brings together the steps through to one-click consolidation.

Rule control is also becoming more granular: Entries can depend on entities, groups, or conditions; substitutions support capital consolidation, and configurable sign logic reduces external conversions. This means less file-based logic, clearer rules, and better auditability.

For 2026, planned developments include IFRS 18 updates, additional source fields and conditions in reporting rules, and improvements to Data Collection. Greater automation in portfolio and group structure management is intended to reduce maintenance effort and errors when structures change frequently.

Five Questions That Must Be Answered Before Choosing a Tool

  1. Which source systems supply reported data? Fully account for S/4HANA instances, non-SAP systems, non-financial data, and manual submissions.
  2. Where should consolidation be operated? Evaluate the stand-alone and ERP-integrated models in the context of governance and compliance, as well as release strategy and integration requirements.
  3. Which reporting logic must be retained? Document reporting items, rules, hierarchies, derivations, and special logic from SEM-BCS or BW.
  4. What belongs in Group Reporting, and what belongs in Datasphere? Clearly separate consolidation logic, data provisioning, and analytical models.
  5. Which roadmap functions are essential for the target architecture? Explicitly identify announced functions as dependencies and plan a robust interim solution.

A Sustainable Target Architecture Starts with the Process, Not the Product

The starting point is a functional assessment: Where do waiting times, manual rework, or gaps in traceability occur? This is used to create a prioritized process view.

Next, it is defined for each data source how it will be connected, transformed, and validated. Group Reporting Data Collection covers manual submissions as well as file-, API-, and OData-based submissions. SAP BDC and Datasphere handle data provisioning and modeling, while SAP Analytics Cloud provides reports, dashboards, and, depending on the scenario, group planning as well.

A phased implementation reduces risk: Start with a limited scope for the financial close and a small number of prioritized reports. Test data lineage, rules, validations, and the audit trail end to end before adding further entities, planning data, or non-financial information.

Conclusion: Replacing SEM-BCS Is Also an Architectural Decision

SAP S/4HANA for Group Reporting is more than the technical replacement for a consolidation landscape that is being phased out. Together with SAP Datasphere and SAP BDC, it can enable corporate reporting that connects financial data, consolidation, planning, and analysis on a common data foundation.

The benefits only emerge through clearly defined data flows, reporting logic, and responsibilities. The key question is therefore not, “Which tool will replace our current system?” but rather, “How do we create a financial close process in which every figure is quickly available, functionally explainable, and technically traceable?”

entry.title: How to Extract Large Volumes of SAP Pricing Data into SAP Datasphere Without Running Out of Memory
entry.content:
If you have ever tried to pull sales pricing condition records from SAP S/4HANA into SAP Datasphere using a generic OData connection and hit a TSV_TNEW_PAGE_ALLOC_FAILED short dump, you are not alone. High-volume pricing tables are one of the most common sources of memory failures in OData-based extraction. This post documents a tested solution: pagination for the initial full load and filter-based delta extraction for ongoing refreshes.

The Problem

The S/4HANA OData service API_SLSPRICINGCONDITIONRECORD_SRV exposes sales pricing condition records across multiple entity sets. When the underlying tables hold millions of rows — which is typical in any production system with complex pricing — a single unbounded OData GET request forces the ABAP application server to allocate all result rows into memory at once. The runtime error TSV_TNEW_PAGE_ALLOC_FAILED is the ABAP kernel's way of saying it ran out of roll area before it could return the response.

The knock-on effect is that neither the initial load nor any subsequent refresh completes successfully, leaving the Datasphere local table empty or stale.

 

Solution Overview

The fix has two parts that address different phases of the data pipeline:

  • Pagination in Datasphere for the initial full load — prevents S/4 from building one giant result set in memory.
  • Filter-based delta extraction for daily refreshes — uses an S/4 OData feature to retrieve only records changed within a configurable time window.

Part 1: Initial Full Load with Pagination

Connection Settings

Create or reuse a generic OData connection in Datasphere pointing to the S/4 communication arrangement URL. Set the OData version to V2, which is what API_SLSPRICINGCONDITIONRECORD_SRV exposes.

Data Model

The pricing API splits condition records across entity sets by validity type (date-dependent, quantity-based, and so on). The recommended data model is a union of those validity entities, then joined to the main record entity. This mirrors the logical structure of the underlying ABAP condition tables and avoids cartesian joins.

 

 

Data Flow Configuration

Open the data flow and configure three areas:

  1. Data Flow level: Dynamic Memory Allocation

Enable this setting. Pricing condition data is wide and joins amplify row width further. Without dynamic allocation, the Datasphere execution engine can exhaust its default memory ceiling before the run finishes.

  1. Source node: Fetch Size and Batch Query

In the properties of the OData source node, enable Fetch Size and Batch Query. This activates server-side pagination. When the data flow starts, Datasphere first sends a $count request to learn the total row count, then issues sequential OData calls using $top and $skip to page through the result set in manageable chunks. Neither call ever asks S/4 to extract all rows simultaneously, which eliminates the memory pressure that triggered the short dump.

Example paging sequence emitted by Datasphere:

GET .../A_SlsPrcgConditionRecord/$count

GET .../A_SlsPrcgConditionRecord?$top=50000&$skip=0

GET .../A_SlsPrcgConditionRecord?$top=50000&$skip=50000

...

  1. Target node: Update Records By Primary Key (UPSERT)

 Enable UPSERT on the target node. This makes reruns safe: if a run is interrupted and restarted, already-written records are updated rather than duplicated. It also makes the same flow reusable for delta loads.

Part 2: Delta Extraction for Daily Refreshes

The S/4HANA Feature: NumberOfDaysSinceCreation , NumberOfDaysSinceLastChange

API_SLSPRICINGCONDITIONRECORD_SRV exposes a virtual filter property called NumberOfDaysSinceCreation , NumberOfDaysSinceLastChange on the A_SlsPrcgConditionRecord entity. Setting it to 1 returns only records that were created or modified in the last calendar day, without any custom ABAP code on the S/4 side.

Delta OData request:

GET /sap/opu/odata/sap/API_SLSPRICINGCONDITIONRECORD_SRV/A_SlsPrcgConditionRecord?$filter=NumberOfDaysSinceLastChange eq 1

You can parameterise this value in the Datasphere data flow to control the lookback window. Set it to 2 or 3 on Mondays to catch weekend changes.

Delta Data Model

For the delta flow, union two sets of records:

  • Records filtered by creation date (new records).
  • Records filtered by last-change date (updated records).

Both branches expand to the validity entity. In the OData source node properties, set Depth to 2. This instructs Datasphere to issue $expand to the associated validity entity in the same OData call, avoiding a separate roundtrip.

The target is the same local table used by the full load. With UPSERT enabled, changed records overwrite existing rows and new records are inserted cleanly on every scheduled run.

Monitoring the Runs

After starting a data flow run, open the data flow in Data Builder and switch to the Monitoring view. Two tabs are available:

  • Messages: execution log entries, warnings, and error details.
  • Metrics: row counts processed per source and target node, memory consumed, and elapsed time per stage.

For the paginated initial load, watch the row counter in Metrics increment in batches. This confirms that $top/$skip cycling is working rather than a single unbounded fetch that would trigger the memory error again.

Summary

Four settings in Datasphere and one S/4 OData feature eliminate the memory crash and enable a sustainable incremental load pattern:

  • Dynamic Memory Allocation on the data flow: prevents Datasphere-side memory exhaustion on wide, joined result sets.
  • Fetch Size + Batch Query (pagination) on the OData source: breaks S/4 reads into bounded $top/$skip pages, preventing TSV_TNEW_PAGE_ALLOC_FAILED.
  • UPSERT on the target: makes reruns and delta merges idempotent.
  • NumberOfDaysSinceLastChange filter: offloads delta filtering to S/4 with zero custom code.

The same pattern applies to any high-volume OData entity in S/4HANA. If you are hitting memory errors on a different service, start with pagination and dynamic memory allocation. Those two settings alone resolve the majority of cases.

Remark

During the OData service execution in the S/4 backend, you may not only run out of memory, but also encounter processing timeouts, e.g. 10 mins. In this case, you may need to create an additional source entity with different filters in your data flow. Or even a different data flow.
